cards.title: A stronger separation between secret sharing and monotone real formulas
cards.formal: Can the separation in Theorem 19 be improved? The source exhibits n-variable authorization functions computable by monotone real formulas of size O(n), but requiring normalized total share size Ω(n²/log n) in every perfect secret-sharing scheme. It asks for a larger gap between these complexity measures. A general lower bound above n²/log n is relevant, but the intended formula-size comparison and precise asymptotic target still need specification.
cards.why: Would show a sharper distinction between succinctly recognizing authorized groups and realizing their access policy with perfect information-theoretic privacy, clarifying the limitations of monotone computation as a proxy for secret-sharing complexity.
cards.status_note: Read the original definitions, separation and full ECCC version. Confirmed the June 2026 journal publication, but could not access its full text. The claim was not independently proved or formally checked; the separation target also remains underspecified.

importance.reason: A structural comparison between unrestricted perfect privacy and monotone real computation, with relevance to general secret-sharing barriers. Existing score retained.

sentences: This problem compares the size of monotone real formulas with the total information needed for perfect secret sharing of the same access structure.
The source gives linear formula size and a nearly quadratic total-share lower bound.
It seeks a larger separation, but does not fix the precise strengthened comparison.
An August 2026 preprint claims a quadratic general share lower bound without supplying the corresponding small-MRF separation.
The card therefore records the new claim and the remaining formulation issue separately.

cards.definitions: An access structure on n parties is represented by a nonconstant monotone Boolean function f:{0,1}ⁿ→{0,1}: A⊆[n] is authorized when f(1_A)=1, and authorization is preserved by adding parties. A perfect secret-sharing scheme has a finite secret alphabet S with |S|≥2 and finite share alphabets S₁,…,Sₙ. Its randomized dealer assigns to each secret s a distribution on S₁×⋯×Sₙ. For every authorized A, the marginal supports for distinct secrets are disjoint, so the shares indexed by A determine the secret exactly. For every unauthorized A, those marginal distributions are identical for all secrets. No computational restrictions, linearity assumptions, error or statistical leakage are allowed. All logarithms are base two. The total share size is Σᵢlog|Sᵢ|, and its normalized value is Σᵢlog|Sᵢ|/log|S|. Let SS(f) be the infimum of this normalized value over all perfect schemes and all finite secret alphabets. A monotone real formula is a finite rooted binary tree whose leaves are Boolean input variables (repetitions allowed) and whose internal gates compute arbitrary coordinatewise nondecreasing functions R²→R. Its output must equal f(x) for every Boolean input x, although intermediate values may be real. Size counts every gate, including every input occurrence; the gate functions have no bit-complexity or computability restriction in this model. Let MRF(f) be the minimum such size. These are separate measures: computing who is authorized need not implement a secret-sharing scheme. The reference separation has MRF(fₙ)=O(n) and SS(fₙ)=Ω(n²/log n).
cards.answer_criterion: Specify the strengthened asymptotic comparison intended by the source and prove the required upper bound on MRF complexity together with the lower bound on SS for the same access-structure family. A lower bound against only linear or efficient schemes, a one-share/total-share confusion, or merely a bound on the size of currently known constructions is insufficient. The exact improvement threshold and whether linear MRF size must be retained remain unresolved formulation choices.

context_blocks.title: Recognizing authorization and enforcing privacy are different tasks
context_blocks.text: A small formula can determine which groups are authorized. A secret-sharing scheme must also distribute correlated information so every authorized group can recover the secret while every other group learns nothing. The source measures the gap between these requirements.

context_blocks.title: The comparison already goes beyond Boolean formula size
context_blocks.text: Real gates can apply arbitrary monotone functions to real intermediate values. The known linear-size MRF and the lower bound for unrestricted perfect sharing therefore compare two substantially different notions of representation.

context_blocks.title: The historical lower-bound barrier has a new claimed advance
context_blocks.text: An August 2026 preprint claims normalized total share entropy Ω(n²) for an explicit family, improving the historical general lower bound by a logarithmic factor. Entropy is at most log alphabet size, so the claimed bound also implies a total-share-size bound. This is recorded as a preprint claim, not an independently verified resolution.

context_blocks.title: That claim is not yet the stated separation comparison
context_blocks.text: The new paper presents an O(n²)-size Boolean formula for its family, and does not give the small-MRF versus large-share theorem needed to compare with Theorem 19. The original paragraph must not be reduced to the general share lower-bound question alone.

context_blocks.title: Remaining formulation issue
context_blocks.text: The source observes that improving its separation would require an ω(n²/log n) general total-share lower bound, but does not state a quantified separation conjecture. It leaves open whether the intended target retains an O(n)-size MRF, asks for a larger ratio of the two minimum complexities with unrestricted MRF size, or specifies another growth rate. Fix that comparison and its asymptotic quantifiers before certifying a single yes/no benchmark. The newly claimed general Ω(n²) bound does not by itself determine the missing formula-size comparison.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
